section.title: Praise the Lord, O My Soul
section.sectionRationale: The first of the Psalter's closing Hallelujah psalms. It moves from a resolve to praise for life, through a warning against trusting mortal princes, to the LORD's own resume of compassionate justice for the oppressed, hungry, prisoners, blind, and bowed down, the very works Jesus points to as signs of the kingdom, Luke 7:22, Matthew 11:5.
section.thesis: Mortal rulers cannot save and their plans perish with them, but the LORD who made heaven and earth executes justice, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, opens blind eyes, lifts the bowed down, and reigns forever, works fulfilled in Jesus and consummated when He returns as Zion's eternal King.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a resolve to praise for life, verses 1-2; a warning against trusting mortal princes, verses 3-4; blessedness in the God of Jacob and His compassionate works for the oppressed, verses 5-9; and the LORD's eternal reign over Zion, verse 10.

units.label: Praise the Lord, O my soul
units.note: a resolve to praise for life

verses.text: {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}! Praise the LORD, O my soul.
I will praise the LORD all my life; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being.

units.label: Put not your trust in princes

verses.text: Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save.
When his spirit departs, he returns to the ground; on that very day his plans perish.

units.label: Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob
units.note: the LORD's compassionate justice for the oppressed

verses.text: {{ashrei|Blessed}} is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God,
the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. He remains faithful forever.
He executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free,
the LORD opens the eyes of the blind, the LORD lifts those who are weighed down, the LORD loves the righteous.
The LORD protects {{ger|foreigners}}; He sustains the fatherless and the widow, but the ways of the wicked He frustrates.
The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations. {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}!

haleluyah.gloss: An imperative call, praise the LORD (Yah, a short form of Yahweh). It opens and closes each of the last five psalms, framing the whole Psalter's final movement as one continuous shout of praise.

ashrei.gloss: Blessed, happy, or fortunate. The same word opens Psalm 1; true blessedness is found not in princes but in the God of Jacob, whose help never fails.

ger.gloss: A foreigner or resident alien living among God's people. The LORD's justice extends beyond Israel to the vulnerable outsider, named here alongside the fatherless and the widow.

basic.context: This psalm opens the five closing Hallelujah psalms of the Psalter, 146 to 150. It moves from a private resolve to praise, to a warning against trusting mortal rulers, to a hymn of the LORD's compassionate justice for the oppressed, hungry, imprisoned, blind, bowed down, and foreign, culminating in His eternal reign over Zion.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a wisdom psalm of trust, contrasting mortal princes, whose plans perish at death, with the eternal God whose faithful works never fail. The abiding call is exclusive trust in the LORD rather than in any human power, however impressive.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens and closes with haleluyah, praise the LORD. Verse 5 pronounces ashrei, blessed, on the one whose help is the God of Jacob. Verse 9 names the ger, the foreigner, among those the LORD protects, widening His justice beyond Israel's own borders to the vulnerable outsider.
basic.typology: The LORD's works in verses 7 to 9, justice for the oppressed, food for the hungry, freedom for prisoners, sight for the blind, lifting for the bowed down, are the very works Jesus names as signs of the kingdom when John's disciples ask if He is the one to come, Luke 7:22 and Matthew 11:5, and the works He reads from Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue, Luke 4:18-19.
basic.christ: Jesus is the LORD's compassion in the flesh. He reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue and claims its fulfillment, then later answers John's disciples by pointing to the blind seeing, the lame walking, and the poor hearing good news, the very list this psalm gives as proof of who He is, and of who reigns forever over Zion.
basic.god: God is shown as the only trustworthy helper, eternal and faithful, who acts in justice and compassion for the oppressed, hungry, imprisoned, blind, bowed down, righteous, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and who reigns forever as Zion's King, in contrast to mortal princes whose plans perish.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:18-19 shows Jesus reading Isaiah 61 and claiming the ministry of justice, sight, and freedom this psalm ascribes to the LORD. Luke 7:22 and Matthew 11:5 show Jesus pointing to these same works as proof of His identity. Revelation 11:15 and Daniel 7:14 echo the psalm's confession that the LORD reigns forever.
basic.oneStory: This is the LORD's own resume of compassionate justice, fulfilled when Jesus, God come near, does these very things in flesh and blood, and fulfilled fully when He returns to reign forever as Zion's true King.

context.literary:
Psalm 146 is the first of five psalms that close the Psalter, 146 to 150, and each of them begins and ends with the same shout, hallelujah. Together they are a crescendo: the opening psalm praises with a single voice, and by Psalm 150 everything that has breath is summoned. This first one is built on a sharp turn. Verses 1 to 4 speak in the first person and then to the congregation, a vow followed by a warning. Verses 5 to 10 answer the warning with a beatitude, and then fill it with a run of descriptions of the LORD.

Notice how the psalm talks to itself. It begins by addressing the singer's own soul, as Psalms 103 and 104 do, before it addresses anyone else. The vow of verse 2 uses two lines that say the same thing in two ways, 'all my life' and 'while I have my being,' so that praise is tied to the whole span of the singer's existence. Then verse 4 supplies the reason the vow is wise: the princes of verse 3 have a lifespan, and the singer is going to outlive their promises by singing to the One who does not.

The long central stretch, verses 6 to 9, is a chain of short clauses, most of them led by the LORD as subject, and the name is repeated three times in verse 8 alone. The effect is of a hand moving down a list, case by case. The order is not random. It begins with the cosmic claim, the Maker of heaven and earth, and ends with the folded hands of the widow and the foreigner. Between them the clauses move from those wronged, to the hungry, to the shut up, to the blind, to the bowed, and then to the righteous, so that the God of the whole creation is shown at the bedside of the least. The last line of verse 9 turns the list on its head, the one place where the psalm names an opponent, and verse 10 closes the frame with a royal declaration to Zion.
context.historical:
The psalm has no title and gives no name of author or occasion, so the setting has to be read from its concerns. The warning in verse 3 would have rung differently in a nation with kings. Israel's story is full of princes who were trusted and then died: Saul on Mount Gilboa, 1 Samuel 31:4-6, and Josiah at Megiddo, 2 Chronicles 35:23-24, are only two. The prophets repeatedly spoke against trust in political and military arrangements. Isaiah says, 'Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils,' Isaiah 2:22, and Isaiah 31:1-3 denounces those who go to Egypt for horses and chariots instead of looking to the Holy One of Israel. Psalm 118:8-9 and Psalm 62:9-10 stand in the same line. Many readers place Psalm 146 after the exile, when Israel had learned that kings and empires come and go, but the psalm itself would have been a fit hymn in any generation that was tempted to rest its hope on the strong.

The people named in verses 7 to 9 are the ones the law singled out for protection. In an agrarian society without welfare, the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner held no land and had no family to defend them in court. Deuteronomy 10:18 describes the LORD in almost the very terms of this psalm: 'He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing.' The law then commands Israel to do likewise, Deuteronomy 10:19 and Leviticus 19:33-34. A judge who is bribed, a landowner who ignores the gleaning law, or a king who takes more than his share, as Samuel warned, 1 Samuel 8:11-17, is acting against the character of the God Israel sings about.

The title 'God of Jacob' in verse 5 would also have carried history. Jacob was the supplanter who fled with a staff and nothing else, Genesis 32:10, and who found help from God he had not expected. To call the LORD the help of Jacob is to say that He helps those who have little else, and the word help was shaped in that story.
context.canonical:
Psalm 146 is lifted straight from the vocabulary of the rest of the Old Testament. The warning about princes is found in Psalm 118:9, Isaiah 2:22, and Jeremiah 17:5-8, which sets the person who trusts in mankind beside the one who trusts the LORD, like a shrub in the desert beside a tree planted by water. The line about the spirit departing and the man returning to the ground is a deliberate echo of Genesis 3:19 and Ecclesiastes 12:7. The works of verses 7 to 9 are found again in Psalm 68:5-6, Psalm 113:7-9, and Psalm 145:14-20, and the psalm that comes just before this one, Psalm 145, ends with the line about the wicked that this psalm repeats in its own words. The two are best read together: Psalm 145 praises the King, and Psalm 146 shows the King at work.

In the Prophets the same acts are promised as signs of the coming age. Isaiah 35:5-6 foresees the eyes of the blind opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped, Isaiah 42:6-7 gives the Servant the task of opening blind eyes and bringing prisoners out of the dungeon, and Isaiah 61:1 sends the anointed one to bring good news to the poor and freedom to the prisoners. What the psalm says the LORD does, the prophets say the LORD will do through His chosen servant.

In the New Testament the connection is explicit. Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus reading from Isaiah and declaring that it is fulfilled that day. When John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the One to come, the answer in Luke 7:22 lists works, not titles: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the poor have good news preached to them. The final line of the psalm, 'The LORD reigns forever,' is taken up in Revelation 11:15, where the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of 'our Lord and of His Christ,' and in the angel's word to Mary, Luke 1:33, 'His kingdom will never end.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his hearers to make a choice and to feel why it is a choice at all. The warning in verse 3 is not cynicism about government or about people. It is a statement about what any human being is able to carry. 'Who cannot save' says that the people we most want to lean on lack the power of rescue, not the will. The psalm presses the point with the sharpest fact it has, the day on which a ruler's spirit departs and his plans stop with him, verse 4. The man who built his hope on that ruler is left with an unfinished project and a buried patron.

The hearers are then invited to see what the other option looks like. Instead of arguing, the psalmist describes. He gives a list of what the LORD actually does, and he lets the hearers recognise their own neighbours in it: a prisoner, a blind beggar, a widow with no one to speak for her, a stranger who has no land. A first hearer who was one of these would have heard the list as a promise addressed to them, and a hearer who was comfortable would have heard it as a charge, since the God who does these things looks for people who do them as well. The psalm closes by turning the camera from the individual to the nation. The personal vow of verse 2 widens into a statement over Zion that the King is not going to die, so that the community is told that its security does not hang on the next succession.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this psalm is description, and what it describes is what the LORD does. Prescription sits in two places only: the opening commands to praise, and the implied command of verse 3, do not trust princes. That distinction guards against two opposite mistakes. One reads verse 3 as a ban on political life, as though the believer must not serve in government or trust a doctor or a judge. The psalm is about ultimate trust, and the Bible elsewhere honours rulers and officials as God's servants, Romans 13:4. The other mistake reads verses 7 to 9 as a promise that every prisoner will be freed and every blind person will see in this life. The psalm lists what God does, it does not promise that each case will come out one particular way today.

What carries forward is the shape of the life that fits the description. People who worship a God who lifts the bowed down are asked to look at who is bowed down in their own street. James 1:27 puts care for orphans and widows at the centre of pure religion, and Matthew 25:35-40 treats hunger, strangers, and prisoners as the places where the King is met. The psalm makes believers into people whose hands resemble their God's.

debates.question: What does verse 4 mean when the man's spirit 'departs' and 'he returns to the ground'?

views.label: The ordinary end of every human life
views.case: The verse echoes Genesis 3:19 and Ecclesiastes 12:7. It simply states the limit of the mortal rulers of verse 3. Nothing is said here about what happens to the person afterward, only about the end of the plans. The shorthand 'that very day' stresses how sudden and complete the stop is.

views.label: A statement that says nothing about life after death
views.case: Some argue that the psalm is making its point only about the loss of earthly power, and deliberately leaves the afterlife outside its scope. Its contrast is between the prince who cannot save and the God who can, not between two kinds of afterlife.

debates.bearing: Either way the verse is about the limits of human power. The psalm does not need a full doctrine of the afterlife to make its case, and later Scripture fills that doctrine in, as Isaiah 26:19 and John 11:25 show.

debates.question: Who are 'the righteous' and 'the wicked' in verses 8 and 9?

views.label: Two moral camps within Israel and the nations
views.case: The psalm uses 'the righteous' and 'the wicked' as the Psalter does everywhere, to name those who live in loyalty to God and those who live against Him. The LORD loves the first group and frustrates the second, so that the two groups face opposite outcomes.

views.label: The oppressed and the oppressors
views.case: Set beside the long list of vulnerable people in verses 7 to 9, 'the wicked' are read as those who exploit them. The wicked are then defined by what they do to the poor, and the righteous by what the LORD does for them.

debates.bearing: The two readings overlap. Verse 9 puts the wicked directly after the widow and the fatherless, which supports the second view, while the Psalter's wider use of the terms supports the first. In either case the psalm refuses to treat God's love as a neutral stance toward wrong.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 5 opens with ashrei, the same beatitude word that begins the whole Psalter in Psalm 1:1. It is plural in form and is often read as an exclamation of the happy state of the person it names. Psalm 1 sets blessing on the one who delights in the law, and Psalm 146 places it on the one whose help is the God of Jacob. The word 'help' is ezer, the word God uses of the woman in Genesis 2:18 and the psalmist uses in Psalm 121:2, where help comes from the LORD, 'the Maker of heaven and earth,' the same title that stands in Psalm 146:6. The ezer is not a junior assistant. In several places it is God Himself who is the help, which is why the word suits the psalm.

The word translated 'save' in verse 3 is teshuah, from the root of yeshua, and it means rescue or deliverance. 'Who cannot save' is literally that the mortal has no deliverance in him. The same root becomes the name Jesus, the Greek form of Yeshua, and that makes the verse sound more than it first appears: the psalm says that no prince has salvation, and the gospel says that the name above all names does. The phrase 'mortal man' in verse 3 is ben adam, 'son of Adam,' and verse 4 says that he returns to the adamah, the ground. The wordplay recalls Genesis 2:7 and 3:19, and it reminds the reader that the one who is called a son of Adam is made of the same stuff as his subjects.

Verses 6 to 9 are driven by participles. The LORD is described as 'the One who makes,' 'the One who keeps,' 'the One who gives,' 'the One who sets free,' 'the One who opens,' and 'the One who lifts.' The Hebrew participle describes ongoing, characteristic action rather than a single past event, so the psalm is not recounting a few famous rescues. It states what God is always doing. The BSB's 'remains faithful forever' translates a participle of shamar, to keep or guard, followed by the word for truth or faithfulness. The same verb shamar returns in verse 9, where the LORD 'protects' foreigners, so the God who keeps faith keeps the stranger as well.

The 'weighed down' of verse 8 is a word from the root meaning to bend, kafaf, and the identical word appears in Psalm 145:14, 'lifts up all who are bowed down.' The two psalms are neighbours, and the shared word ties them together. In verse 9 the LORD 'sustains' the fatherless and widow with a verb, ye'odded, that is also used of the LORD in Psalm 147:6. The final clause says that the way of the wicked He 'frustrates.' The verb carries a picture of bending or twisting, so that the road of the wicked is made crooked and does not arrive where they intended.

The Septuagint numbers this psalm as 145, and Psalm 147 is divided into two, so that the English Psalm 147:12 begins the Greek Psalm 147. A reader looking up a Greek or Latin reference to 'Psalm 145' will be looking at this psalm.

typology.type: The LORD who opens the eyes of the blind, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The prophets set the opening of blind eyes among the signs of the age to come, Isaiah 35:5 and Isaiah 42:7, and the psalm already says that the LORD does it. In the Gospels the correspondence is lived out. Jesus gives sight to blind men and in John 9 He says that the man was born blind so that the works of God might be displayed in him, John 9:3, and that He is the light of the world, John 9:5. The escalation is that the one who opens eyes is now present in person, and the sight He gives reaches beyond the body, John 9:39. The type falls short of the end: not every blind person is healed in the Gospels, and the full removal of every blindness waits for the age to come.

typology.type: The LORD who sets prisoners free, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The psalm pictures release for the shut up and condemned, as in Psalm 102:19-20, and the prophets give the work to the Servant, Isaiah 42:7 and Isaiah 61:1. In Nazareth Jesus applies it to Himself, 'to proclaim liberty to the captives,' Luke 4:18. The deeper release is from the power of sin and death, which Hebrews 2:14-15 describes as freeing those who were held in slavery by fear of death. The type is partial because many literal prisoners, including John the Baptist, stayed in their cells, Matthew 11:2, so the freedom that Christ brings is first of all the freedom of the heart and finally the freedom of the resurrection.

typology.type: The LORD who sustains the fatherless and widow, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The law ties God's care for the fatherless and widow to His own character, Deuteronomy 10:18, and the psalm repeats the claim. The church of Acts takes it up as a community practice, caring for widows in Jerusalem, Acts 6:1-6, and James names the care of orphans and widows as the mark of pure religion, James 1:27. In Christ the correspondence deepens, for He provided for His own mother from the cross, John 19:26-27, and He promises, 'I will not leave you as orphans,' John 14:18. The type falls short of the fullness of that gift until the age when God will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:4.

typology.type: The King who reigns forever over Zion, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's closing declaration sets a King who does not die against the princes of verse 3. David's line was promised an everlasting throne, 2 Samuel 7:13, but every son of David in the Old Testament died, which is what verse 4 would predict. The gap is closed in the son of David who was raised. Gabriel says of Jesus that He will reign over the house of Jacob forever and that His kingdom will never end, Luke 1:32-33. The pattern is therefore fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and enthronement, though its public completion waits for the day when every enemy is put under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the sort of King it describes. A King who reigns forever and who helps the helpless is a King that David's dynasty could not provide by itself, because every ruler in that line eventually reached verse 4. The New Testament says that Jesus is the son of David who does not die. Luke 1:32-33 uses the very language of an unending reign over the house of Jacob, and Hebrews 7:16 and 7:25 speak of a priest who lives by the power of an indestructible life and who always lives to intercede. What Psalm 146 asks Israel to believe about the LORD, the Gospels show in the body of the Son.

It leads to Christ by the works the psalm lists. When John sends from prison to ask, 'Are You the One who was to come?' Luke 7:19, Jesus does not argue from titles. He points to what has been seen and heard: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor, Luke 7:22. That list is made from Isaiah's promises, Isaiah 35:5-6, 26:19, 29:18-19, and 61:1, and it overlaps the list of Psalm 146:7-9. The answer carries an astonishing implication: the One doing the works that belong to the LORD is the LORD come near. Matthew 11:5 gives the same list, and Mark 1:41 shows the temper in which He does them: moved with compassion, He reached out and touched a leper.

It leads to Christ by the hunger and the feeding. 'He gives food to the hungry' becomes the feeding of the five thousand, John 6:5-13, in which the Lord who provides is standing among the hungry crowd and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Jesus also speaks of Himself as the one who is met in the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner, Matthew 25:35-40, so that the psalm's care for the weakest becomes the place where the King is found.

It leads to Christ by the contrast of verses 3 and 4 with the cross and the empty tomb. Princes die and their plans perish. Jesus died, and for a day it seemed His plans had perished too, as the Emmaus road shows, but the plan did not stop at the grave, Acts 2:24. Herod accepted the praise of a god and was struck down, Acts 12:21-23, while the Lord accepted the praise of children and fishermen and rose.

A word of caution is wise. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and it is not a veiled prediction of Jesus. Its direct subject is the LORD. The New Testament makes the connection because the Son does the LORD's works and is acknowledged with the LORD's name, so the link is by identity and shared action, not by hidden code. The warning of verse 3 also applies to any attempt to treat a church leader, a party, or a movement as a saviour. Jesus is the only prince in whom the psalm allows trust, and He is the one whom the psalm does not call a prince at all, but the King who reigns forever.
study.god:
The first thing this psalm shows is a God whose help is bigger than any rescuer and a trust that lasts as long as He does. He is introduced as 'the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them,' verse 6, and the whole list that follows depends on that. The same hand that set the heavens in place is the one that lifts the bent back of one person. The psalm does not let power and tenderness be separated, and it supports the point by joining the two in a single sentence.

He is faithful in a way no human leader can be. 'He remains faithful forever' stands in deliberate contrast with 'his plans perish' in verse 4. The word for faithful is the language of truth and of guarding, and it is the character Psalm 145:13 describes when it says that the LORD is faithful in all His words. His word is not an election promise that lapses with the term of office.

He is just, and His justice is specific. He 'executes justice,' mishpat, for the oppressed, and the psalm does not leave that abstract. It names bread, release, sight, and a lifted head. This tells us that justice in the Bible is not only the tidy resolution of a court case but the rescue of people who have been left out. The psalm also names the foreigner, a reminder that God's care is not limited to Israel's own, which is consistent with Deuteronomy 10:18.

He is a God who loves. The phrase 'the LORD loves the righteous' stands in the middle of the list, and the word love is the plainest affective word in the psalm. Love is not set against justice here but sits alongside it, as the motive of a God who acts for people.

He is a God who frustrates evil. The last line of verse 9 acts as a hinge. A God who only comforted the weak and left their oppressors untouched would not be good, and the psalm does not picture such a God. What He does to the wicked is described as making their way crooked, so that they do not get where they are going. The verse refuses to let the care for the poor become a sentimental picture.

He is King. Verse 10 uses the verb that means to reign, in a form that stretches over time, and it adds 'for all generations,' so that kingship is not a title but a continuous act.

For worship the psalm turns praise into an ongoing conversation with oneself: 'Praise the LORD, O my soul.' It teaches that praise is partly an act of resolution, a way of pledging the whole of one's life to the One who can hold it, and partly an act of honesty, saying out loud that no leader can bear the weight we want to place on him. It also teaches the worshipper where to look. The one who worships this God is turned toward the prisoner, the hungry, and the foreigner, because that is where the God of verse 7 can be seen at work.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah tells Israel to stop trusting in man, who has only breath in his nostrils. It is the prophetic form of Psalm 146:3-4, and it shows that the warning was a settled strand of Israel's teaching, not a passing mood of one psalmist.

A short proverb of the same kind, 'It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.' It closes the group of festival psalms that begins at Psalm 113, so Psalm 146 repeats a creed that Israel sang at its pilgrim feasts.

Jeremiah turns the choice into two pictures. The one who trusts in mankind is a shrub in a salt land, and the one who trusts the LORD is a tree by a stream that does not worry in a year of drought. It explains why Psalm 146 begins with a blessing for the second kind of person.

The psalm just before this one says that the LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down. The same Hebrew word for bowed down appears in Psalm 146:8, so the two psalms read as a pair, the first praising the King and the second showing His works.

Moses describes the LORD as the One who executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. It is the law behind verse 9, and it ends with a command that Israel should do the same, since they were foreigners in Egypt.

Another hallelujah psalm that praises the LORD for raising the poor from the dust and giving the barren woman a home. The theme of reversal here, where the lowly are seated with princes, takes up the same contrast between princes and the poor that drives Psalm 146.

The prophet foretells that the eyes of the blind will be opened and the lame will leap like a deer when God comes to save. It places the psalm's works of verses 7 to 9 inside Israel's hope for the coming age, which is why Jesus answers John with this list.

The anointed one is sent to preach good news to the poor and proclaim freedom to the prisoners. Jesus reads this text in Nazareth, and its pairing of the poor and the prisoners is the same as that of Psalm 146:7.

Jesus's reply to John's question about whether He is the One to come lists the blind, the lame, the lepers, the deaf, the dead, and the poor. He cites works instead of titles, and the works are the LORD's own, which is the claim the psalm invites.

The King says that what was done for the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner was done for Him. The psalm's care for the weakest becomes the place where the Son is met, and those who copy the LORD's works find themselves serving the King.

Pure and undefiled religion, James says, is to care for orphans and widows in their distress. It turns verse 9 into the daily practice of the people of God, so that the worship of the LORD and the care of the helpless are not separate concerns.

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, who will reign forever and ever. It is the final fulfilment of the psalm's last line, that the LORD reigns forever, and it shows the Christ sharing that reign.

study.oneStory:
This psalm answers a question that runs through the whole story of Scripture: where can people safely put their hope? The garden began with a trust that was broken, Genesis 3:4-6, and the Bible from then on is the story of humanity looking for rescuers. Pharaoh promised bread in Egypt and delivered slavery. Israel asked for a king to judge them 'like all the other nations,' 1 Samuel 8:5, and the line of kings that followed produced a few good men and a long run of disasters, ending in the exile. Psalm 146 is what is left standing when the kings have failed: the God of Jacob is the one in whom hope is safe.

It also takes up the story of the exodus. The God who 'sets the prisoners free' is the God who heard the groaning in Egypt and came down, Exodus 3:7-8, and who afterward told Israel to treat the foreigner and the fatherless as He had treated them, Deuteronomy 10:18-19. The psalm gathers that history into a few lines and presents it as a pattern that continues. The poor man who sings it is a child of the slaves who were freed.

The psalm sets up the arrival of the King. By holding up before Israel a God who is King forever, it leaves a gap between the promise of everlasting rule and the actual line of David, whose members all die. The gap is not left open. In Luke the angel announces a son of David whose kingdom will never end, Luke 1:32-33. In Nazareth He reads Isaiah and says that the words are fulfilled in the hearing of His neighbours, Luke 4:18-21. His answer to John in Luke 7:22 rests on the psalm's list. The King came in the form of one who touched lepers and fed the hungry.

The psalm also reaches into the church's life. Because the King reigns, His people are sent to serve those whom He serves, and the early church is marked by that, Acts 6:1-6 and James 1:27. They live in the time between the arrival of the King and the completion of His work, taking the side of those the world forgets.

The story ends where the psalm's last line points. In Revelation 11:15 the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of 'our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.' Daniel 7:14 had pictured a dominion that will not pass away. In the new creation the princes of verse 3 are gone, the tears are wiped away, Revelation 21:4, and the King whose helpers were the helpless sits on a throne in the middle of the city, Revelation 22:3-4. The wicked have no part in it and the blind see his face.

quiz.q: What does Psalm 146 warn against trusting for salvation?

options.text: Princes and mortal man, who cannot save, whose plans perish when they die.
options.note: Verses 3-4 ground the warning in human mortality itself.

options.text: Wealth and riches accumulated in this life.
options.note: A related biblical theme, but this psalm's specific warning is against trusting mortal rulers.

options.text: Idols carved by human hands.
options.note: A real biblical concern elsewhere, but not this psalm's specific target.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm teaches self-reliance.
options.note: The psalm teaches trust in God, not in self or in princes.

quiz.q: What works does the LORD do for the oppressed, hungry, prisoners, blind, and bowed down, verses 7-9?

options.text: He executes justice, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, opens blind eyes, and lifts up the bowed down.
options.note: This sevenfold list of active compassion is the psalm's centerpiece.

options.text: He promises a future reward without acting now.
options.note: The psalm describes present, active works, not merely a future promise.

options.text: He commands the wealthy to help them instead.
options.note: The LORD Himself is the subject of every verb in this passage.

options.text: He ignores them until the final judgment.
options.note: The opposite is true; the LORD acts for them now.

quiz.q: How does Jesus point to Psalm 146's language of God's compassion?

options.text: By pointing to His own healing of the blind, lifting the bowed down, and good news to the poor as proof of His identity, Luke 7:22 and Matthew 11:5.
options.note: Jesus directly echoes this psalm's list when answering John's disciples.

options.text: By quoting Psalm 146 word for word in a parable.
options.note: Jesus alludes to and enacts this list of works rather than quoting the psalm verbatim.

options.text: By rebuking the psalm's hope in worldly deliverance.
options.note: Jesus fulfills, rather than rebukes, this psalm's hope.

options.text: By reserving these works only for the age to come.
options.note: Jesus performs these works in His earthly ministry, though their fullness awaits His return.

quiz.q: Who does the LORD especially protect, according to verse 9?

options.text: The foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
options.note: The ger, foreigner, is named alongside the classic biblical pair, the fatherless and the widow.

options.text: Only the native-born Israelite.
options.note: The verse explicitly includes the foreigner, widening the LORD's protection beyond Israel's own.

options.text: Only kings and princes.
options.note: The psalm has just warned against trusting princes; verse 9 names the vulnerable, not the powerful.

options.text: Only those who prove themselves worthy.
options.note: The LORD's protection here is unearned, extended to the vulnerable by His own character.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's climactic confession in verse 10?

options.text: The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations.
options.note: This closing declaration answers the opening warning against mortal princes whose reigns end.

options.text: Human kings will reign forever.
options.note: The opposite is true; only the LORD's reign is everlasting.

options.text: The world will end in chaos.
options.note: The psalm ends in confident hope, not in chaos.

options.text: God's reign will one day come to an end.
options.note: The verse says the very opposite, that His reign is for all generations.

questions: Where are you tempted to put ultimate trust in a "prince," a leader, a position, a portfolio, or a plan, that cannot ultimately save?
The LORD executes justice for the oppressed and feeds the hungry, verse 7. Where might God be calling you to join His work of compassion this week?
Jesus points to these very works, sight to the blind, freedom to the captive, as signs of His kingdom. How does that shape your hope when your own body or circumstances feel bowed down?
Verse 9 names the foreigner alongside the fatherless and the widow. Who is the vulnerable outsider in your community that this psalm calls you to notice?
The psalm ends, "The LORD reigns forever." What situation in your life needs that reminder right now?

translationNotes.note: Hallelujah renders halelu-yah, an imperative plural, praise Yah; it opens and closes each of the last five psalms of the Psalter.
Spirit renders ruach, which can also mean breath, the same word used of the breath of life in Genesis 2:7, underscoring human frailty apart from God.
Foreigners renders ger, a resident alien; the sense includes any such vulnerable outsider living among God's people.
